Our business is medicine - we contract with hospitals to provide acute care physician staff.

And we do a lot of things to increase our profits. However there are a lot more things we could do. For example some ER doc groups see uninsured patients and then once they have satisfied EMTALA, if there is no emergency medical condition (EMC) they provide no other care or treatment. For example, you bring in your kid who has an ear infection or you come in with a tooth infection. That's a problem, but not an EMC because you can see your doctor tomorrow and it would not be expect to be life or limb threatening if you weren't treated emergently. So these groups will yell you: yep you have an infection, but if you want me to write you a prescription for antibiotics, you'll have to pre-pay X dollars of your bill. Of course most uninsured people are poor and thus don't have the money, so they get seen, EMTALA is satisfied, but they don't get the care they need. Even if they don't provide care, they then send you a bill (because you get billed even if you don't get a prescription - perfectly legal). Then when you can't pay, they sell the bill at pennies on a dollar to collection agencies.

Now the real business model here is to teach the local poor people that unless you have a real emergency, you won't get any help and even if you do, you will be hounded forever by bill collectors for that care. What happens is one hospital in an area does this, and then as though by asshole magic, poor uninsured people don't come in so they have more time to pay attention to 'paying customers' and get them in faster, so more of them come. The other hospitals in the area then have a choice: adopt the asshole business practices or see their waiting rooms fill with the uninsured. Eventually unless there is a public hospital there is effectively no place to go for poor and uninsured people.

However I and my partners, while we want to be compensated, don't want to squeeze out an extra 10% at the expense of our medical ethics. Many ER docs went into the field because they are actually social-justice minded and want to be part of the safety net for those unable to get care elsewhere.
